blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Define a shift of a production possibility curve, and analyse the causes of shifts and the consequences they carry.

blocks.heading: The boundary itself moves
blocks.text: A shift of the PPC moves the whole boundary rather than a point sliding along it. An outward shift shows the economy productive capacity has grown: more of at least one good can be produced than before. An inward shift shows capacity has shrunk. The shift is about what the economy could do, not what it chose: a country that builds workshops and trains technicians has shifted its boundary outward even if its actual output point stays where it was.

blocks.heading: A shift, in figures
blocks.text: A weaving co-operative in Gobabis trains its 15 members on faster looms. Before the training its boundary ran from 90 scarves to 45 blankets a week; after it, the same members and looms can reach up to 120 scarves or 60 blankets a week. The whole boundary has moved outward: 120 - 90 = 30 more scarves and 60 - 45 = 15 more blankets. A combination beyond the old boundary, such as 100 scarves a week, now sits inside the new one. Growth of capacity is shown by the new curve, not by a slide along the old one.

blocks.heading: What moves the boundary
blocks.text: Capacity grows when an economy gains resources or gets more out of them: more workers, more machines, better training, or technology that raises what an hour of work produces. Vietnam two decades of building factories and technical schools have pushed its boundary outward, which is why output once beyond reach is now routine there. Capacity shrinks when resources are destroyed: a flood that washes away looms and yarn shifts the co-operative boundary inward, and the maximum of both goods falls together. The consequences land on consumers, who face whatever the new boundary permits, and on workers, whose jobs depend on the capacity it describes.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Sliding along the boundary is topic 1.4.3 reallocation; the shift of the boundary is how growth of capacity is shown, and the training and saving that buy it carry the opportunity cost of topic 1.3.
